evidence.title: Advanced Technologies for Characterizing and Detecting Battery Thermal Failure: A Review.
evidence.abstract: Energy storage is essential in accelerating the global transition toward clean and sustainable energy across various sectors. Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have become increasingly significant for energy storage due to their high energy density, low maintenance, and high coulombic efficiency. However, a challenge arises from the risk of thermal failure across all cell formats and chemistries, particularly under harsh electrochemical and thermal conditions and mechanical stress. In severe cases, such failures have led to catastrophic fires or explosions, posing substantial safety risks and environmental concerns due to gas emissions and toxic discharge. Therefore, an understanding of thermal failure mechanisms is essential for ensuring the safe deployment of batteries across various applications. This review first examines the causes and consequences of thermal failure, providing didactic mechanistic insights. It then compares recent progress in thermal and electrochemical failure analysis using advanced characterization techniques, including X-ray imaging, optical sensing, acoustic field imaging, and spectroscopy, to study the thermal runaway (TR) mechanism and reveal how thermal failures develop and propagate in batteries. It further examines how these advanced characterization tools can inform battery management systems and industrial practice and concludes by outlining future challenges and perspectives for achieving safe energy storage systems.

evidence.title: Study on the incorporation of phase change material and differently embedded water circulation pipes for enhanced thermal management of photovoltaic system.
evidence.abstract: This research presents an experimental investigation on the thermal management and improvement of electrical efficiency of photovoltaic (PV) systems employing a phase change material (PCM) and water combination technique as heat dissipation systems through an improved design. This experiment was conducted in the semi-arid environment of Aligarh, India. The experiment utilised an aluminium enclosure that housed PCM with a melting point of 30 °C (OM 30), along with integrated water circulation pipes. The study involved the evaluation and comparison of three types of PV systems: a PV system with an empty casing attached to the rear surface, a PV system with a casing filled with PCM, and a PV system with a casing filled with a combination of PCM and water circulated using embedded serpentine pipes (without making contact with the casing walls). The water flow rates used in the study were 0.0027 kg/s and 0.0034 kg/s. Power generation, exergy analysis, power efficiency, and performance metrics, specifically the power increase performance variable of the system were compared. The average increases in electrical efficiency, power output, power enhancement, and maximum average temperature reduction, were found to be 13.75%, 24.14 W, 27.6%, and 5.6 °C, respectively at water flowrate of 0.0034 kg/s (best case). The findings of the study indicate that the improvement in the design concept of the PCM and water combination system results in superior performance of the PV panel compared to other approaches.

evidence.title: Steady-State Characteristic Assessment and Dynamic Performance Testing for a Metal-Supported Solid Oxide Fuel Cell Auxiliary Power Unit with Methanol On-Board Reforming.
evidence.abstract: The highly efficient and low-pollution solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) power generation system offers a clean energy supply solution, playing a significant role in promoting energy transformation and accelerating the development of low-carbon energy. Safe and portable liquid fuels have received extensive attention in mobile SOFC applications due to their excellent fuel versatility. However, the overall performance of the SOFC system is highly dependent on reforming options and operating strategies. In this study, a novel methanol-reforming on-board SOFC auxiliary power unit (APU) system is proposed. The performance of SOFC with methanol under steam and autothermal reforming is evaluated by thermodynamic analysis at 550 °C with 0.3 A/cm 2 current density for a metal-supported SOFC stack. The methanol autothermal reforming (ATR) consumes less heat and shows better start-up performance compared with steam reforming, making it more suitable for the SOFC-APU system. The maximum electrical efficiency of the SOFC system can reach 47.5% with methanol ATR. By optimizing the reforming strategy and operating parameters, the conceptual design of the SOFC-APU system achieves a balance between system efficiency and methanol consumption during the steady operation phase. The simulation results showed that the electrical efficiency of the system reached 52.1% with a 0.46 g/s methanol flow rate at a 70% anode gas recirculation ratio. Based on the above SOFC-APU system, a dynamic series hybrid system with a battery as the main driving power source and an SOFC as an auxiliary power source was designed and simulated. The hybrid system can meet the dynamic and economic requirements, making up for the short mileage and endurance of the electric vehicle. Meanwhile, it reduces the peak power demand of the battery system and prolongs the battery life, showing the development potential of an SOFC in the future transportation field.

evidence.title: System-level thermal and electrical modeling of battery systems for electric aircraft design
evidence.abstract: This work introduces a framework for simulating the electrical power consumption of an 8-seater electric aircraft equipped with high-energy-density NMC Lithium-ion cells. We propose an equivalent circuit model (ECM) to capture the thermal and electrical battery behavior. Furthermore, we assess the need for a battery thermal management system (BTMS) by determining heat generation at the cell level and optimize BTMS design to minimize energy consumption over a predefined flight regime. The proposed baseline battery design includes a 304-kWh battery system with BTMS, ensuring failure redundancy through two parallel switched battery banks. Simulation results explore the theoretical flight range without BTMS and reveal advantages in increasing battery capacity under specific conditions. Optimization efforts focus on BTMS design, highlighting the superior performance of water cooling over air cooling. However, the addition of a 9.9 kW water-cooled BTMS results in a 16.5% weight increase (387 kg) compared to no BTMS, reducing the simulated range of the aircraft from 480 km to 410 km. Lastly, we address a heating-induced thermal runaway scenario, demonstrating the robustness of the proposed battery design in preventing thermal runaway.

system.value: Advanced Technologies for Characterizing and Detecting Battery Thermal Failure: A Review.

abstract.value: Energy storage is essential in accelerating the global transition toward clean and sustainable energy across various sectors. Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have become increasingly significant for energy storage due to their high energy density, low maintenance, and high coulombic efficiency. However, a challenge arises from the risk of thermal failure across all cell formats and chemistries, particularly under harsh electrochemical and thermal conditions and mechanical stress. In severe cases, such failures have led to catastrophic fires or explosions, posing substantial safety risks and environmental concerns due to gas emissions and toxic discharge. Therefore, an understanding of thermal failure mechanisms is essential for ensuring the safe deployment of batteries across various applications. This review first examines the causes and consequences of thermal failure, providing didactic mechanistic insights. It then compares recent progress in thermal and electrochemical failure analysis using advanced characterization techniques, including X-ray imaging, optical sensing, acoustic field imaging, and spectroscopy, to study the thermal runaway (TR) mechanism and reveal how thermal failures develop and propagate in batteries. It further examines how these advanced characterization tools can inform battery management systems and industrial practice and concludes by outlining future challenges and perspectives for achieving safe energy storage systems.

system.value: Study on the incorporation of phase change material and differently embedded water circulation pipes for enhanced thermal management of photovoltaic system.

abstract.value: This research presents an experimental investigation on the thermal management and improvement of electrical efficiency of photovoltaic (PV) systems employing a phase change material (PCM) and water combination technique as heat dissipation systems through an improved design. This experiment was conducted in the semi-arid environment of Aligarh, India. The experiment utilised an aluminium enclosure that housed PCM with a melting point of 30 °C (OM 30), along with integrated water circulation pipes. The study involved the evaluation and comparison of three types of PV systems: a PV system with an empty casing attached to the rear surface, a PV system with a casing filled with PCM, and a PV system with a casing filled with a combination of PCM and water circulated using embedded serpentine pipes (without making contact with the casing walls). The water flow rates used in the study were 0.0027 kg/s and 0.0034 kg/s. Power generation, exergy analysis, power efficiency, and performance metrics, specifically the power increase performance variable of the system were compared. The average increases in electrical efficiency, power output, power enhancement, and maximum average temperature reduction, were found to be 13.75%, 24.14 W, 27.6%, and 5.6 °C, respectively at water flowrate of 0.0034 kg/s (best case). The findings of the study indicate that the improvement in the design concept of the PCM and water combination system results in superior performance of the PV panel compared to other approaches.

system.value: Steady-State Characteristic Assessment and Dynamic Performance Testing for a Metal-Supported Solid Oxide Fuel Cell Auxiliary Power Unit with Methanol On-Board Reforming.

abstract.value: The highly efficient and low-pollution solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) power generation system offers a clean energy supply solution, playing a significant role in promoting energy transformation and accelerating the development of low-carbon energy. Safe and portable liquid fuels have received extensive attention in mobile SOFC applications due to their excellent fuel versatility. However, the overall performance of the SOFC system is highly dependent on reforming options and operating strategies. In this study, a novel methanol-reforming on-board SOFC auxiliary power unit (APU) system is proposed. The performance of SOFC with methanol under steam and autothermal reforming is evaluated by thermodynamic analysis at 550 °C with 0.3 A/cm 2 current density for a metal-supported SOFC stack. The methanol autothermal reforming (ATR) consumes less heat and shows better start-up performance compared with steam reforming, making it more suitable for the SOFC-APU system. The maximum electrical efficiency of the SOFC system can reach 47.5% with methanol ATR. By optimizing the reforming strategy and operating parameters, the conceptual design of the SOFC-APU system achieves a balance between system efficiency and methanol consumption during the steady operation phase. The simulation results showed that the electrical efficiency of the system reached 52.1% with a 0.46 g/s methanol flow rate at a 70% anode gas recirculation ratio. Based on the above SOFC-APU system, a dynamic series hybrid system with a battery as the main driving power source and an SOFC as an auxiliary power source was designed and simulated. The hybrid system can meet the dynamic and economic requirements, making up for the short mileage and endurance of the electric vehicle. Meanwhile, it reduces the peak power demand of the battery system and prolongs the battery life, showing the development potential of an SOFC in the future transportation field.

system.value: System-level thermal and electrical modeling of battery systems for electric aircraft design

abstract.value: This work introduces a framework for simulating the electrical power consumption of an 8-seater electric aircraft equipped with high-energy-density NMC Lithium-ion cells. We propose an equivalent circuit model (ECM) to capture the thermal and electrical battery behavior. Furthermore, we assess the need for a battery thermal management system (BTMS) by determining heat generation at the cell level and optimize BTMS design to minimize energy consumption over a predefined flight regime. The proposed baseline battery design includes a 304-kWh battery system with BTMS, ensuring failure redundancy through two parallel switched battery banks. Simulation results explore the theoretical flight range without BTMS and reveal advantages in increasing battery capacity under specific conditions. Optimization efforts focus on BTMS design, highlighting the superior performance of water cooling over air cooling. However, the addition of a 9.9 kW water-cooled BTMS results in a 16.5% weight increase (387 kg) compared to no BTMS, reducing the simulated range of the aircraft from 480 km to 410 km. Lastly, we address a heating-induced thermal runaway scenario, demonstrating the robustness of the proposed battery design in preventing thermal runaway.

warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-016 (sharpened per CEO Round 58): A proposed latent quantity survives only when (1) identifiability is demonstrated under an EXPLICIT observation/dynamics model with full rank/observability analysis (not naive unknown-count), AND (2) identifiability REMAINS under plausible model uncertainty (each ideal assumption relaxed toward realistic physics and re-tested). A single favorable rank calculation under a convenient model is INSUFFICIENT. A single unfavorable perturbation model is ALSO INSUFFICIENT to claim universal non-identifiability — it only kills the specific estimator tested under that specific perturbation model. The correct procedure: (a) define state, observables, inputs, noise, known/unknown params; (b) build measurement equations; (c) test rank of Jacobian wrt unknown params; (d) perform adversarial model-uncertainty test: relax each assumption toward realistic physics and re-test identifiability under the combined relaxed model; (e) only if BOTH the ideal-model rank AND the adversarial-model rank hold (or constructively fail) can a universal claim (measurable OR non-measurable) be recorded.

Structural identifiability under a convenient model is not enough. When in doubt, the implementation is killed; the scientific question stays open until either (a) a survivor is found or (b) an explicit non-identifiability counterexample is constructed (two physically distinct latent states producing indistinguishable observations under ALL measurement protocols).

warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: Energy storage is essential in accelerating the global transition toward clean and sustainable energy across various sectors. Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have become increasingly significant for energy storage due to their high energy density, low maintenance, and high coulombic efficiency. However, a challenge arises from the risk of thermal failure across all cell formats and chemistries, particularly under harsh electrochemical and thermal conditions and mechanical stress. In severe cases, such failures have led to catastrophic fires or explosions, posing substantial safety risks and environmental concerns due to gas emissions and toxic discharge. Therefore, an understanding of thermal failure mechanisms is essential for ensuring the safe deployment of batteries across various applications. This review first examines the causes and consequences of thermal failure, providing didactic mechanistic insights. It then compares recent progress in thermal and electrochemical failure analysis using advanced characterization techniques, including X-ray imaging, optical sensing, acoustic field imaging, and spectroscopy, to study the thermal runaway (TR) mechanism and reveal how thermal failures develop and propagate in batteries. It further examines how these advanced characterization tools can inform battery management systems and industrial practice and concludes by outlining future challenges and perspectives for achieving safe energy storage systems.

This experiment was conducted in the semi-arid environment of Aligarh, India. The experiment utilised an aluminium enclosure that housed PCM with a melting point of 30 °C (OM 30), along with integrated water circulation pipes. The study involved the evaluation and comparison of three types of PV systems: a PV system with an empty casing attached to the rear surface, a PV system with a casing filled with PCM, and a PV system with a casing filled with a combination of PCM and water circulated using embedded serpentine pipes (without making contact with the casing walls). The water flow rates used in the study were 0.0027 kg/s and 0.0034 kg/s. Power generation, exergy analysis, power efficiency, and performance metrics, specifically the power increase performance variable of the system were compared. The average increases in electrical efficiency, power output, power enhancement, and maximum average temperature reduction, were found to be 13.75%, 24.14 W, 27.6%, and 5.6 °C, respectively at water flowrate of 0.0034 kg/s (best case). The findings of the study indicate that the improvement in the design concept of the PCM and water combination system results in superior performance of the PV panel compared to other approaches.

custody_records.raw_content: The highly efficient and low-pollution solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) power generation system offers a clean energy supply solution, playing a significant role in promoting energy transformation and accelerating the development of low-carbon energy. Safe and portable liquid fuels have received extensive attention in mobile SOFC applications due to their excellent fuel versatility. However, the overall performance of the SOFC system is highly dependent on reforming options and operating strategies. In this study, a novel methanol-reforming on-board SOFC auxiliary power unit (APU) system is proposed. The performance of SOFC with methanol under steam and autothermal reforming is evaluated by thermodynamic analysis at 550 °C with 0.3 A/cm 2 current density for a metal-supported SOFC stack. The methanol autothermal reforming (ATR) consumes less heat and shows better start-up performance compared with steam reforming, making it more suitable for the SOFC-APU system. The maximum electrical efficiency of the SOFC system can reach 47.5% with methanol ATR. By optimizing the reforming strategy and operating parameters, the conceptual design of the SOFC-APU system achieves a balance between system efficiency and methanol consumption during the steady operation phase. The simulation results showed that the electrical efficiency of the system reached 52.1% with a 0.46 g/s methanol flow rate at a 70% anode gas recirculation ratio. Based on the above SOFC-APU system, a dynamic series hybrid system with a battery as the main driving power source and an SOFC as an auxiliary power source was designed and simulated. The hybrid system can meet the dynamic and economic requirements, making up for the short mileage and endurance of the electric vehicle. Meanwhile, it reduces the peak power demand of the battery system and prolongs the battery life, showing the development potential of an SOFC in the future transportation field.
